title: The Infinitive
subtitle: λύειν, λῦσαι — the verbal noun.
objectives: Form the present, aorist, and future infinitives in all voices.
Understand the infinitive as a verbal noun with tense and voice but no person.
Use the infinitive as subject, object, complement, and in indirect statement.

sections.heading: The infinitive
sections.body:
The infinitive is the verbal noun. λύειν means 'to loose' or 'the act of loosing'. The infinitive has tense (present, aorist, future, perfect) and voice (active, middle, passive) but no person or number. It does not take a subject in the nominative; its subject (if expressed) is in the accusative (this is called accusative and infinitive construction, used in indirect statement).

The infinitive is used as the subject or object of a verb, as a complement (completing the meaning of another verb), and in indirect statement.

sections.heading: Infinitive forms
sections.body:
Present active: λύειν (to loose, to be loosing)
Aorist active: λῦσαι (to have loosed, to loose)
Future active: λύσειν (to be about to loose)

Present middle/passive: λύεσθαι (to loose oneself / to be loosed)
Aorist middle: λύσασθαι (to have loosed oneself)
Aorist passive: λυθῆναι (to have been loosed)
Future middle: λύσεσθαι (to be about to loose oneself)
Future passive: λυθήσεσθαι (to be about to be loosed)

The present and aorist infinitives are most common. The future infinitive is less common. The perfect infinitive exists but is rare.

sections.heading: Uses of the infinitive
sections.body:
Subject: λύειν ἐστὶ καλόν — 'To loose is noble' or 'Loosing is noble.'

Object: βούλομαι λύειν — 'I wish to loose.'

Complement: δοκεῖ λύειν — 'He seems to be loosing.' Many verbs (δοκέω, φαίνομαι, μέλλω, δύναμαι) take a supplementary infinitive.

Indirect statement (accusative and infinitive): φησὶ Σωκράτη σοφὸν εἶναι — 'He says that Socrates is wise.' Σωκράτη is accusative (subject of the infinitive), σοφόν is accusative (predicate adjective agreeing with the subject), εἶναι is the infinitive of εἰμί.

sections.heading: From Plato
sections.body:
Plato, Apology 29b: οὐ παύσομαι φιλοσοφῶν.
'I will not cease philosophizing.' φιλοσοφῶν is the present active participle, but the infinitive construction is parallel: οὐ παύσομαι could take the infinitive φιλοσοφεῖν (to philosophize).

items.answer: He says that Socrates is wise.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can form and recognize the present, aorist, and future infinitives of any ω-verb and can translate infinitives in subject, object, complement, and indirect statement uses.
